note: Each entry may omit fields; the loader applies defaults. 'rulings.default' applies to every profile unless a profile key (strict/mainstream/lenient) or a certifier key overrides it.

entries.reason: Swine flesh and its derivatives are explicitly prohibited (Qur'an 2:173, 5:3, 6:145, 16:115).
Rendered pork fat.
Flowing blood is explicitly prohibited.

entries.canonical: Meat of an animal not ritually slaughtered
entries.reason: Land-animal meat is halal only if the animal was ritually slaughtered. An unlabelled or uncertified source cannot be assumed compliant.
entries.ask: Is the meat from a certified halal-slaughtered source?

entries.reason: Khamr (intoxicating drink) is prohibited, including as a recipe ingredient where it is not fully transformed.
Prohibited as an intoxicant. Widely disputed as a residual carrier solvent in flavourings at trace levels; several certifiers permit below 0.1% carry-over, others do not.
entries.ask: Is ethanol present as an intoxicating ingredient or only as a residual flavour carrier, and at what level?

entries.reason: Conventionally extracted into an ethanol carrier (commonly 35% alcohol) which remains in the product.
entries.ask: Is this an alcohol-free / glycerin-based vanilla extract?

entries.reason: Produced by acetic fermentation of wine. Most schools hold that full transformation to vinegar (istihalah) renders it permissible; a minority reject vinegar deliberately made from wine.
Fully fermented to acetic acid; no intoxicant remains.
A by-product of brewing. The yeast itself carries no intoxicant, though strict standards avoid brewing by-products.
Collagen hydrolysate from animal skin and bone. Porcine is the most common commercial source worldwide; bovine gelatine is halal only from ritually slaughtered cattle.
entries.ask: What species is the gelatine from, and was bovine material halal-slaughtered?

entries.reason: Animal connective tissue; same source question as gelatine.
entries.ask: What species is the collagen from?

entries.reason: Milk-coagulating enzyme. Microbial and plant rennet are halal; calf rennet requires ritual slaughter, and pepsin-based rennet may be porcine.
entries.ask: Is the rennet microbial, plant, or animal? If animal, from what species and slaughter?

entries.reason: A cheese-making by-product; inherits the ruling of the rennet used to coagulate the milk.
entries.ask: What rennet was used in the cheese the whey came from?

entries.reason: A digestive enzyme most commonly harvested from porcine stomach mucosa.
entries.ask: Is the pepsin porcine, bovine, or microbial?

entries.reason: Frequently animal-derived (calf, lamb or kid glandular tissue), though microbial lipase is common.
entries.ask: Is the lipase microbial or animal-derived?

entries.reason: Enzymes may be microbial, plant or animal. Labels rarely disclose which.
entries.ask: What is the source organism for each enzyme used?

entries.reason: Produced by microbial fermentation without animal tissue.
A dough conditioner historically produced by hydrolysing keratin from human hair, duck and chicken feathers, or hog bristle. Synthetic and fermentation-derived L-cysteine is now also available.
entries.ask: Is the L-cysteine synthetic/fermentation-derived, or keratin-hydrolysed?

entries.reason: A red pigment extracted from the cochineal insect. Schools differ on consuming insects: the Maliki position permits, while Hanafi and Shafi'i scholars generally prohibit non-locust insects. Certifiers are divided.
entries.ask: Can the colour be substituted with a plant-based red (e.g. anthocyanin, beetroot)?

entries.reason: A resin secreted by the lac insect, dissolved in ethanol for application. Two separate concerns: insect origin and the alcohol solvent, most of which evaporates.
entries.ask: Is the glaze shellac or a plant/carnauba wax alternative?

entries.reason: A bee secretion, not the insect body; permitted by consensus.
Plant-derived wax from the carnauba palm.
Explicitly praised in the Qur'an (16:69).
A by-product of fat splitting or soap manufacture; the feedstock may be plant oil, petrochemical, or animal tallow including porcine.
entries.ask: Is the glycerol of vegetable, synthetic, or animal origin?

entries.canonical: Mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids
entries.reason: Emulsifier built from glycerol and fatty acids; both components may be animal-derived. One of the most frequently encountered doubtful additives.
entries.ask: Are the fatty acids and glycerol of vegetable origin?

aliases: acetic acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
citric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
mono- and diacetyl tartaric acid esters
entries.reason: Built on the same mono/diglyceride backbone as E471, so it carries the identical fatty-acid source question.
entries.ask: Are the underlying fatty acids of vegetable origin?

entries.reason: Fatty acid salts; source may be tallow or vegetable oil.
entries.ask: Are the fatty acids of vegetable origin?

entries.reason: Commercially derived from either vegetable oils or animal tallow.
entries.ask: Is the stearic acid of vegetable or tallow origin?

entries.reason: Very common tablet lubricant; the stearate may come from tallow or from palm/vegetable oil.
entries.ask: Is the stearate vegetable-sourced?

entries.reason: Contains a stearoyl group whose fatty acid may be animal-derived.
entries.ask: Is the stearic acid vegetable-sourced?

entries.reason: Sorbitan esters of fatty acids; the fatty acid component may be tallow-derived.
entries.ask: Are the fatty acids vegetable-sourced?

entries.reason: Fatty acid esters of sorbitol; fatty acid source may be animal.
entries.ask: Are the fatty acids vegetable-sourced?

entries.canonical: Sucrose esters and polyglycerol esters of fatty acids
aliases: propylene glycol esters of fatty acids
entries.reason: Fatty-acid-based emulsifiers with the same source question. PGPR (E476) is usually castor-oil derived and often halal, but the polyglycerol component traces back to glycerol.
entries.ask: Are the fatty acids and glycerol vegetable-sourced?

entries.reason: Overwhelmingly soy or sunflower derived, both halal. Egg lecithin is also halal. Listed as doubtful only because unqualified 'lecithin' does not state the source; when the label says soy or sunflower it is halal.
entries.ask: Is the lecithin soy, sunflower, or egg?

entries.reason: Made from animal bone; species and slaughter are almost never disclosed.
entries.ask: From what species is the bone phosphate, and was it halal-slaughtered?

entries.reason: Usually synthesised chemically, but can be produced by hydrolysing animal collagen or gelatine.
entries.ask: Is the glycine synthetic or animal-derived?

entries.reason: Extracted from bovine or porcine bile.
entries.ask: What species is the bile from?

entries.reason: Nucleotide flavour enhancers historically extracted from sardines or meat; modern production is often microbial fermentation.
entries.ask: Are the ribonucleotides fermentation-derived or from animal/fish tissue?

entries.reason: Produced by bacterial fermentation; the growth medium and any enzyme used in it are the point of doubt, not the glutamate itself.
entries.ask: What fermentation medium and processing aids are used?

entries.reason: Named after ox bile, from which it was first isolated, but commercial taurine is synthetic.
From hair, feathers, hooves or horn; species and, for human hair, permissibility are at issue.
entries.ask: What is the keratin source?

entries.reason: A secretion from beaver castor sacs, occasionally used in flavourings. The beaver is not ritually slaughtered.
Animal glandular secretions used in aroma compounds.

A legal category, not a single substance. In the US (21 CFR 101.22) it may include material derived from meat, dairy, eggs, or seafood, and commonly uses ethanol or propylene glycol carriers. Nothing on the label narrows it.
entries.ask: Are any flavour components animal-derived, and is ethanol used as a carrier?

entries.reason: Synthetic aroma chemicals are themselves halal, but they are routinely delivered in an ethanol or propylene glycol carrier.
entries.ask: What carrier solvent is used in the flavour system?

entries.reason: Condensed wood smoke; plant-derived.
Derived from cultured yeast, not from brewing.

Usually from lanolin (sheep wool grease, halal by majority view since it is a secretion not flesh) or from fish oil; occasionally stabilised in a gelatine matrix, which reintroduces the gelatine question.
entries.ask: What is the D3 source, and is the beadlet gelatine-coated?

entries.reason: Synthetic retinol is halal, but the palmitate ester and the gelatine-based beadlet coating used for stability are both source-dependent.
entries.ask: Is the vitamin A preparation gelatine-coated?

entries.reason: The pigments themselves are plant or microbial. The doubt is the delivery form: fat-soluble carotenoids are often supplied as gelatine-encapsulated beadlets.
entries.ask: Is the colour supplied in a gelatine-encapsulated form?

entries.reason: Fish and sea creatures are permitted; the Hanafi school restricts this to fish specifically, which covers standard fish oil. Note that softgel capsules are commonly gelatine.
entries.ask: If in capsule form, what is the capsule shell made of?

entries.reason: Capsule shells are gelatine unless stated as HPMC/vegetarian.
entries.ask: Is the capsule gelatine or HPMC/pullulan?

entries.reason: Enzyme from egg white; eggs of halal birds are permitted.
A fish-swim-bladder fining agent; halal in itself, though its main use is clarifying beer and wine.

Sugar itself is halal. Some US and UK cane refiners decolourise with bone char, which does not remain in the product; most scholars and certifiers permit it, a strict minority avoid it. Beet sugar never uses bone char.
entries.ask: Was the sugar refined using bone char?

entries.reason: Charred animal bone used as a decolourising filter medium.
Plant-derived carbon black; the EU permits only vegetable sources for E153.
Unqualified animal fat gives neither species nor slaughter method.
entries.ask: What species is the fat from and was it halal-slaughtered?

entries.reason: A milk protein. Acid casein is halal outright; rennet casein inherits the rennet question.
entries.ask: Is this acid casein or rennet casein?

entries.reason: Coagulated with rennet, which may be microbial, plant, or animal. Some PDO cheeses (e.g. Parmigiano Reggiano) mandate calf rennet.
entries.ask: What rennet was used?

entries.reason: Milk of halal animals is permitted.
Eggs of permitted birds are halal.
'Modified' refers to chemical or physical treatment of plant starch, not genetic or animal modification. Commonly and wrongly flagged as doubtful.
Plant carbohydrate.
Enzymatically hydrolysed plant starch.
Produced by Aspergillus niger fermentation of a sugar substrate.
Despite the name, commercial lactic acid is produced by bacterial fermentation of sugars, not from milk or meat.
Produced by fermentation and chemical synthesis from glucose.
Ascorbic acid esterified with palmitic acid, whose source may be animal fat although palm oil dominates.
entries.ask: Is the palmitic acid vegetable-sourced?

entries.reason: Extracted from vegetable oils or synthesised.
Plant polysaccharide from citrus peel and apple pomace; the standard halal replacement for gelatine.
Seaweed, seed and tree-exudate polysaccharides.
Plant fibre derivatives.
Sugar alcohols produced by hydrogenating plant sugars. Despite the name they are not intoxicants.
Synthetic or plant-derived sweeteners with no animal input.
Synthetic or fermentation-derived preservatives with no animal-source concern. E235 natamycin and E234 nisin are microbial.
Mineral-sourced phosphates. Note this is distinct from E542 bone phosphate, which is animal-derived.
Synthetic, mineral or plant colours with no animal input. E101 riboflavin is fermentation-produced; a small number of strict standards query its growth medium.
Inorganic mineral salts and acids.
Propylene glycol is petrochemical and halal. Note that E1517/E1518 are glycerol acetates, so they carry the glycerol source question.
entries.ask: For glyceryl acetates, is the glycerol vegetable-sourced?

entries.reason: Plant-derived oils.
Plant-derived proteins and cereals.
Mineral and plant seasonings.
Plant-derived.
Plant-derived.
Plant-derived.
The Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools permit all sea creatures. The Hanafi school permits only fish, treating shellfish as impermissible; shrimp is disputed even within it.
entries.ask: Does the consumer follow the Hanafi position on non-fish seafood?

entries.reason: Fish are permitted across all schools and require no ritual slaughter.
Insects other than locusts are impermissible in the majority view.
Water is pure and permitted.
Poultry is halal in itself but only if ritually slaughtered. Uncertified poultry cannot be assumed compliant.
entries.ask: Was the poultry halal-slaughtered, and by which certifier?

entries.reason: Cattle, sheep and goats are halal species but require ritual slaughter.
entries.ask: Was the meat halal-slaughtered, and by which certifier?

entries.reason: Stock may be built on uncertified meat or bone.
entries.ask: What animal material is the stock made from and was it halal-slaughtered?

entries.reason: Plant-derived cereals.
